title: Export Readiness (Selected Products): From Local Seller to First Export Shipment
subtitle: Prepare one product you already make, such as dried ginger, hibiscus or adire, for a foreign buyer with the right paperwork, label, price and shipment plan.
description: A hands-on advanced course for producers who already sell locally and want to export one selected product. You will choose a product and market with real calculations, build your Nigerian export base, write a spec sheet and export label, price with Incoterms 2020, check buyers and payment terms, and finish with a dated 90-day readiness plan.
outcomes: Choose an export product and first market using freight-share calculations and a weighted scorecard
List and start the Nigerian registrations and product documents your export needs (CAC, NEPC, Form NXP, NAQS, NAFDAC or SON)
Write an export specification sheet, lot system and destination-compliant label draft
Build an export price from cost to an FCA or CIF quote with a currency buffer
Verify buyers, choose safe payment terms and prepare a matching invoice, packing list and shipment checklist
Produce a costed 90-day export readiness plan
audience: Women producers who already sell a product consistently in Nigeria and want to prepare it for buyers in another country.
tools: Smartphone with WhatsApp and a browser
Your product, its current label and packaging
Your CAC and other business documents

modules.title: Choosing the Product, the Market and the Paperwork Base
modules.overview: Not every product should travel, and not every country is a sensible first market. In this module you test your products against export criteria, score possible markets with a simple weighted method, and check the Nigerian registrations and permits you need before any foreign buyer can receive your goods.

lessons.title: Which of your products can travel: value per kilogram, shelf life and supply
objectives: Calculate how much freight adds to the price of each product you make
Judge a product's shelf life, fragility and regulatory class for export
Check whether you can supply the same quality again and again
Choose one product to prepare for export first

blocks.text: Exporting means a buyer in another country receives your goods legally, in good condition, at a price that still pays you. The first decision is not the country. It is the **product**. A product that sells well in Ibadan may be a poor export because it is heavy for its price, spoils quickly, breaks in transit or falls under strict rules abroad. A small, light, stable product can travel well even from a home workshop.

blocks.name: earth-globe-europe-africa
blocks.alt: A globe showing Africa and Europe
blocks.caption: Before choosing a country, choose the product that can survive the journey and still make money.

blocks.text: Five tests for an export product

items: **Value per kilogram.** Freight is charged mostly by weight or size. A product worth a lot per kilogram (a hand-dyed adire scarf) carries freight easily. A cheap, heavy product (dried zobo leaves, raw shea nuts) needs sea freight and large volumes to make sense.

**Shelf life and stability.** Sea freight from Lagos to Europe and customs clearance can take weeks. A product must stay safe and attractive for the whole journey and then for months on a shop shelf. Dried, low-moisture goods (dried ginger, sesame, hibiscus calyces) travel better than fresh pepper or wet pastes.
**Fragility.** Glass jars and liquid soaps leak and break. Textiles and dried goods in sealed bags rarely do.

**Regulatory class.** Food, cosmetics and anything you swallow or put on skin face the strictest rules abroad. Crafts and textiles usually face fewer product rules, though labelling and customs rules still apply.

**Repeatable supply.** A buyer who likes your sample will ask for the same thing again, often in larger quantity. You must know where your raw materials come from and how much you can make per month without quality dropping.

blocks.text: Freight as a share of price

A quick way to compare products is to ask: if I sent one unit by air, what share of my local price would the freight eat? You need three numbers: the **gross weight** of one packed unit (product plus its packaging), an **air freight rate per kilogram** quoted by a forwarder or courier, and your **local selling price**. Divide the freight per unit by the price. A share above about half is a warning sign for air freight. It does not kill the product, but it tells you that product needs sea freight, bulk packing or a much higher foreign price.

blocks.title: Worked example: three products, one freight rate
blocks.context: For example, Funmi in Abeokuta makes a 250 g shea body cream in a glass jar (local price about N4,000), 1 kg bags of dried zobo leaves (about N3,000) and hand-dyed adire scarves (about N15,000). A forwarder has quoted her, for example, N8,000 per kg by air to London. All prices are approximate and only for practice.
steps: She weighs one packed unit of each: the cream jar with lid and box weighs 0.40 kg, the zobo bag in its outer pouch 1.10 kg, the folded scarf in a sleeve 0.20 kg.
Freight per unit: cream 0.40 x 8,000 = N3,200; zobo 1.10 x 8,000 = N8,800; scarf 0.20 x 8,000 = N1,600.
Freight as a share of local price: cream 3,200 / 4,000 = 80%; zobo 8,800 / 3,000 = about 293%; scarf 1,600 / 15,000 = about 10.7%.

She then checks the other tests. The cream is a cosmetic in glass: fragile and, for the UK and EU, it needs a responsible person based in that market. The zobo is stable but very cheap per kg. The scarf is light, unbreakable and not a food or cosmetic.
blocks.result: Funmi chooses the adire scarf as her first export product. She keeps zobo as a later sea-freight product to sell in bulk with other producers, and decides the cream needs more groundwork before it can travel.

blocks.title: Where your products sit
items: High value, light rules: start here
High value, strict rules: plan carefully
Low value, light rules: bulk by sea
Low value, strict rules: wait
axes: How strict the product rules are
blocks.caption: Products in the top-left box are usually the easiest first exports; bottom-right products need volume, partners and compliance first.

blocks.text: Shelf life you can prove

Buyers abroad will ask for your **shelf life** and how you know it. A guess is not enough. For dried foods, keep dated samples in their final packaging at room temperature and check them every month for smell, colour, insects and clumping. For anything regulated by NAFDAC, the shelf life on your registered label is the one to use. Write down what you observe. That written record is part of what makes you export ready.

blocks.title: Do not over-promise volume
blocks.text: A buyer may ask, 'Can you supply 2 tonnes a month?' Answer with the number you can actually make at the same quality, based on your last three months of production and your raw material supply. Promising more and failing on the second order damages trust far more than a smaller honest answer.
A simple capacity check

Look at your records for the last three months. How many units did you make in your best month and in your worst month? What stopped you making more: raw materials, drying space, hands, money or electricity? The worst month, not the best, is the safe number to offer a new export buyer. If you have no records, start counting now; the Simple Record-Keeping course on the WODDI Institute shows easy methods.

Finally, think about **who else** could help you reach volume. Many first exports from small producers happen when several women who make the same product to the same specification pack together under one name or through a cooperative. You will plan this in Module 3. For now, choose one product, not five. Export readiness is detailed work, and doing it well for one product teaches you the method for all the others.

takeaways: Choose the product before the country: value per kg, shelf life, fragility, rules and supply
Freight per unit divided by price shows quickly which products suit air freight
Light, stable, high-value, lightly regulated products are the easiest first exports
Offer buyers the volume of your worst recent month, not your best

activity.title: Score your products for export
steps: List up to three products you make and their current local price
Weigh one packed unit of each on a kitchen scale and write the weight in kg
Ask one forwarder or courier for an air rate per kg to one country, or use N8,000 per kg for practice
Calculate freight per unit and freight as a percentage of price
Note shelf life evidence, fragility, product class and your worst-month output for each
Choose one product and write two sentences explaining why
activity.evidence: A one-page table or notebook photo showing the calculations and your chosen product

lessons.title: Picking one target market with HS codes, trade data and a weighted scorecard
objectives: Find the HS heading for your product and explain why it matters
Use free trade-data tools to see who buys your product and what duties apply
Compare buyer types: diaspora shops, importers and online buyers
Score three possible markets with a weighted scorecard and choose one

blocks.text: Once you have a product, you need **one** first market. Trying to sell to 'the world' wastes data, money and time. You will look at three things for each possible country: is there demand for your product there, how hard are the product rules, and how easy and costly is it to get goods there and get paid.
Your product's customs name: the HS code

Every product crossing a border is classified with a number from the **Harmonized System (HS)**, maintained by the World Customs Organization. The first six digits are the same in every member country. Countries add more digits for their own tariff lines. Customs officers, freight forwarders, the trade-data tools below and the buyer's import duty all depend on this code, so getting it right is the first technical job.

head: Product
HS heading or subheading
What it covers
rows: Sesame seeds
Sesamum seeds, whether or not broken
Cashew nuts
0801.31 (in shell) / 0801.32 (shelled)
Fresh or dried cashew nuts
Dried ginger
0910.11 (whole) / 0910.12 (crushed or ground)
Ginger
Soap such as black soap
Soap and organic surface-active products in bars and similar forms

blocks.title: Confirm the full code
blocks.text: The table gives headings to show how the system works. Before you quote or ship, confirm the full national tariff line for both Nigeria and the buyer's country with your freight forwarder or the buyer's customs tariff. Two similar products, for example whole and ground ginger, can sit on different lines with different duties.
Free tools to look at demand and duties

items: **Trade Map** (trademap.org, by the International Trade Centre): shows which countries import your HS code, how much and from whom. Look for countries whose imports are steady or growing.
**Market Access Map** (macmap.org, also by the International Trade Centre): shows the import duty and many other requirements a country applies to your HS code from Nigeria.
**Access2Markets** (the European Commission's portal) for the EU, the **UK Trade Tariff** on GOV.UK for the United Kingdom, and the **US FDA** website for food going to the United States.
**NEPC** (Nigerian Export Promotion Council): market information, export training and buyer matching for registered exporters.

blocks.name: map
blocks.alt: A person studying a large map with location pins
blocks.caption: Research narrows 'the world' down to one market you can actually serve well.

blocks.text: Three kinds of buyers

**Diaspora shops and caterers** abroad already know products such as dried zobo, ogiri, ginger and adire. They buy small quantities and may accept a simple label, but they still must obey their country's import and labelling law. **Importers and distributors** buy larger volumes, ask for specifications, test reports and consistent supply, and often put your product on their customer list. **Online buyers** ordering one item at a time are possible for light products such as textiles and crafts, using courier services, but each parcel carries its own customs and delivery costs.

For food, two rules stand out. In the **EU and UK**, prepacked food must carry specific information in a language consumers there understand, and the 14 major allergens must be emphasised. In the **United States**, FDA requires food facilities that make, process, pack or hold food for US consumption to register, and requires **prior notice** to be submitted for imported food shipments. Inside **ECOWAS**, neighbouring markets such as Ghana are closer and cheaper by road, and the ECOWAS Trade Liberalisation Scheme exists for approved originating products. Ask NEPC whether your product qualifies before relying on it.
Scoring markets with weights

A **weighted scorecard** turns your research into a choice. Pick four or five criteria, give each a weight that adds up to 100%, score each country from 1 (poor) to 5 (good) and multiply. Score rule difficulty so that **easier** rules get a **higher** score, so that every high number is good.

blocks.title: Worked example: three markets for dried ginger
blocks.context: For example, Amina in Kaduna dries and packs ginger. She is choosing between the UK (diaspora shops), Ghana (wholesalers in Accra) and the USA. Her weights: demand 30%, ease of rules 25%, logistics cost 20%, buyer contacts 25%.
steps: UK scores: demand 5, rules 2, logistics 2, contacts 4. Total = 0.30x5 + 0.25x2 + 0.20x2 + 0.25x4 = 1.5 + 0.5 + 0.4 + 1.0 = 3.40.
Ghana scores: demand 3, rules 4, logistics 5, contacts 3. Total = 0.9 + 1.0 + 1.0 + 0.75 = 3.65.
USA scores: demand 4, rules 2, logistics 1, contacts 3. Total = 1.2 + 0.5 + 0.2 + 0.75 = 2.65.
She checks the weights add up: 30 + 25 + 20 + 25 = 100%.
blocks.result: Ghana scores highest (3.65), so Amina prepares for Ghana first and keeps the UK (3.40) as her second market once her labels and test reports are ready.

blocks.title: From product to chosen market
items: Confirm the HS code
Check imports in Trade Map
Check duties and rules
Identify real buyer types
Score with weights
Choose one market
blocks.caption: Each step narrows the list until one market is left that you can research properly.

blocks.text: Write down every source you used and the date you looked. Duties and rules change, and you will need to recheck them before your first shipment.

takeaways: The HS code drives duties, data searches and customs paperwork, so confirm it early
Trade Map shows who imports your product; Market Access Map shows duties and requirements
Diaspora shops, importers and online buyers want different volumes and documents
A weighted scorecard with weights adding to 100% turns research into a clear choice

activity.title: Build your market scorecard
steps: Write the HS heading you believe fits your product and one question to confirm with a forwarder
Choose three possible countries and note the buyer type you would target in each
Look up each country on Trade Map or Market Access Map and note one fact about demand or duty
Set weights for four criteria that add to 100% and score each country from 1 to 5
Multiply, add, and circle the winner
activity.evidence: A scorecard table with your sources and the date you checked them

lessons.title: Your Nigerian export base: CAC, NEPC, Form NXP, regulators and an honest gap check
objectives: List the Nigerian registrations and documents a small exporter normally needs
Identify which regulator covers your product: NAFDAC, NAQS or SON
Run an honest gap check on your own business
Spot the warning signs of common export scams

blocks.text: Before a buyer abroad can receive your goods, you must be able to send them legally from Nigeria. The exact list depends on your product and destination, but most small exporters build the same base. Think of it as the foundation under a house: buyers rarely see it, but nothing stands without it.

blocks.name: passport-control
blocks.caption: Your goods need their own 'passport': registrations and documents that let them leave Nigeria and enter the buyer's country.

blocks.text: The common Nigerian base

head: Item
Who handles it
Why it matters
rows: Registered business name or company
Corporate Affairs Commission (CAC)
Banks, NEPC and buyers expect to deal with a registered business, not a personal name
Exporter registration certificate
Nigerian Export Promotion Council (NEPC), online e-registration and renewal
Identifies you as a registered exporter and opens NEPC services such as market information and buyer matching
Nigerian Export Proceeds Form (Form NXP)
Your bank, under Central Bank of Nigeria rules
Records the export and the expected foreign payment so that proceeds can come back through the banking system
Product-specific permits and certificates
NAFDAC for regulated food and cosmetics; NAQS for plant products; SON for standards certification
Prove the product is safe, healthy or standard as the buyer's country requires
Certificate of origin
Issuing body depends on destination and scheme; ask NEPC or your forwarder
Shows where goods were made, which can affect duty in the buyer's country

blocks.text: Which regulator covers your product?

items: **Plant products** such as dried ginger, sesame, hibiscus calyces, cashew and shea nuts: the importing country often asks for a **phytosanitary certificate**, issued in Nigeria by the **Nigerian Agricultural Quarantine Service (NAQS)** after inspection.

**Processed food and cosmetics** such as packaged spice mixes, shea creams and soaps: these are NAFDAC-regulated products in Nigeria. Ask NAFDAC what export documents your buyer's country needs, for example evidence that the product is registered and sold legally in Nigeria.
**Manufactured goods and textiles**: SON's MANCAP certification shows conformity to a Nigerian Industrial Standard. Some buyers and markets ask for it; others ask for their own standards.
The **buyer's country** has the final word. Ask your buyer in writing which documents their customs and food or product authority will ask for.

blocks.title: Export base checklist
items: CAC registration in place
NEPC exporter certificate current
Bank ready to process Form NXP
Product regulator identified
Buyer's required documents listed
blocks.caption: Tick each line only when you hold the document or have written confirmation.

blocks.text: An honest gap check

Export work is less forgiving than local trade. At home, a customer may accept a missing date or a bag that is slightly light. Abroad, a missing certificate can hold goods at the port while storage charges grow, or lead to the goods being refused and destroyed. The habit you need is **precision**: check every document, number and spelling against the buyer's instructions, twice.

blocks.title: Worked example: a gap check for dried ginger to Ghana
blocks.context: For example, Amina (from the last lesson) is preparing ginger for Accra wholesalers. She lists what she has and what she lacks.
steps: Has: CAC business name registration, a business bank account, records of six months of production.
Lacks: NEPC exporter registration. Action: register online on the NEPC e-registration portal this month.
Unknown: whether the Ghanaian buyer needs a phytosanitary certificate and an ECOWAS certificate of origin. Action: ask the buyer by email and ask NEPC and NAQS which apply.
Lacks: a written product specification. Action: write one (Module 2, Lesson 1).
She counts: 3 items in place, 3 to close, 1 question to answer.
blocks.result: Amina's honest list shows four actions, each with an owner and a month. She now knows her real distance from a first shipment instead of guessing.

blocks.title: Money scams that target new exporters
blocks.text: Be very careful with any 'buyer' who promises a large order and then asks you to pay a fee first, for example for an import licence, a 'registration with our ministry', inspection, or a lawyer they choose. Real buyers do not ask suppliers to pay their import permits. Also beware of cheques or transfers for more than the invoice with a request to send back the difference. Verify the company (for UK companies you can search Companies House free online), speak by video call, and never send goods on credit to a first-time buyer you cannot verify.
Questions to put to your buyer in writing

items: Which documents will your customs and food or product authority ask for at import, and who issues each one?
Whose name and address must appear on the label and on the import documents?
Which Incoterm and named place do you prefer, and which port or airport will you use?
Do you need laboratory test reports, and for which tests?
How will you pay, and in which currency?

blocks.text: A written answer protects you. If a buyer later says a document was missing, you can show what they asked for. If a buyer cannot answer these basic questions about their own country, treat that as a warning sign and slow down.

Keep all your certificates in one folder, paper and scanned, with the expiry or renewal date written on the front page. When a buyer asks, you can send clear scans the same day. That speed and order is itself a signal that you are a serious exporter.

takeaways: Most small exporters need CAC registration, NEPC exporter registration and Form NXP through their bank
NAQS, NAFDAC and SON cover different products; the buyer's country decides what it needs
Ask your buyer in writing which documents their authorities require
Never pay fees to a 'buyer' or ship on credit to an unverified first-time buyer

activity.title: Run your own gap check
steps: Copy the export base checklist into your notebook
Mark each line: have it, do not have it, or not sure
For each gap, write one action, who will do it and the target month
Scan or photograph the documents you already hold into one folder with renewal dates noted
activity.evidence: Your completed gap check list and a photo of your organised document folder

quiz.q: Funmi's 250 g cream weighs 0.40 kg packed and sells for N4,000. Air freight is N8,000 per kg. What share of the price does freight take?
quiz.explain: 0.40 x 8,000 = N3,200. 3,200 / 4,000 = 0.8, so 80%. That is a warning sign for air freight.

quiz.q: A buyer asks Bisi how many kilograms of dried hibiscus she can supply monthly. Her output was 300 kg, 220 kg and 260 kg in the last three months. What should she offer?
options: As much as the buyer wants
quiz.explain: The worst recent month is the safe number. Promising more and failing on a repeat order damages trust.

quiz.q: Why is the HS code one of the first things to confirm?
options: It is only needed for food products
It decides the product's colour coding on the label
Customs classification, import duty and trade-data searches all depend on it
It replaces the need for a certificate of origin
quiz.explain: The HS code classifies the product for customs, sets the duty line and is how tools like Trade Map and Market Access Map find data.

quiz.q: In a weighted scorecard, Country A scores demand 4, rules 3, logistics 3, contacts 2 with weights 30%, 25%, 20%, 25%. What is its total?
quiz.explain: 0.30x4 + 0.25x3 + 0.20x3 + 0.25x2 = 1.2 + 0.75 + 0.6 + 0.5 = 3.05. Adding the raw scores (12) ignores the weights.

quiz.q: A new 'buyer' offers a big order but asks Ngozi to first pay for an import licence through his agent. What should she do?
options: Pay quickly so she does not lose the order
Pay half now and half later
Refuse the fee, verify the company independently and treat it as a likely scam
Ship the goods first to show good faith
quiz.explain: Real buyers handle their own import permits. Up-front fee requests are a classic export scam.

quiz.q: Which body issues phytosanitary certificates for plant products such as dried ginger leaving Nigeria?
quiz.explain: The Nigerian Agricultural Quarantine Service inspects plant products and issues phytosanitary certificates when the importing country requires them.

modules.title: Specification, Export Labels and an Export Price
modules.overview: Foreign buyers judge you on paper before they taste or touch anything. This module turns your product into a written specification and a repeatable order process, prepares a label and carton that meet the destination's rules and survive transit, and builds an export price from cost to an Incoterms quote.

lessons.title: Writing an export product specification and a step-by-step export order process
objectives: Write a one-page product specification a foreign buyer can check
Use lot numbers and retained samples so every shipment can be traced
Check net weights against the declared quantity using a sample
Map the stages of an export order from enquiry to payment

blocks.text: A **product specification** (spec sheet) is a written description of exactly what the buyer will receive. Importers ask for it before ordering, compare deliveries against it, and use it if there is a dispute. It also disciplines your own production: if it is written down, you and your helpers can make it the same way every time.

blocks.name: clipboard
blocks.alt: A clipboard holding a written sheet
blocks.caption: A clear spec sheet on one page answers most of a buyer's first questions.

blocks.text: What goes on a spec sheet

head: Section
What to write
Example for dried hibiscus calyces
rows: Product name and HS code
Common name, and the code you confirmed
Dried hibiscus (Hibiscus sabdariffa) calyces, whole
Description
Form, colour, cut, origin
Whole dark red calyces, sun-dried on raised mesh, from Kano and Jigawa farms
Quality limits
What is allowed and not allowed, agreed with the buyer
No live insects, no mould, foreign matter (sand, stones, stalks) below the limit the buyer sets; moisture below the buyer's agreed maximum
Packing
Inner bag, outer pack, quantity per carton or sack
1 kg food-grade sealed bags, 12 bags per carton
Labelling
What is printed and where
Label per destination rules (next lesson) plus lot number
Storage and shelf life
Conditions and how you know
Cool, dry place away from sunlight; shelf life from your dated monthly checks
Documents available
What you can supply
Phytosanitary certificate, certificate of origin, lab report if requested

blocks.title: Agree numbers with the buyer
blocks.text: Limits such as maximum moisture or foreign matter differ between buyers and markets. Do not invent them. Ask the buyer for their specification, or for the standard they use, and copy their numbers into your sheet. If you cannot measure something yourself, name the laboratory you will use.
Lot numbers and retained samples

Give each production batch a **lot number**, for example HB-2611-03 meaning hibiscus, November 2026, third batch. Print it on every bag and carton. Keep a **retained sample** of each lot, around 200 g in a sealed, labelled bag, stored like the product, until well after the buyer has sold it. If a complaint arrives months later, you can open the retained sample and see whether the fault started with you or happened later in transit or storage.
Checking that bags are not under weight

Weight problems are one of the fastest ways to lose an importer. Use a digital scale that you check against a known weight, and weigh a random sample from each lot before packing cartons. Record every weight. Look at both the **average** and the **lowest** bag.

blocks.title: Worked example: ten bags from one lot
blocks.context: For example, Hauwa in Kano packs 1 kg bags of dried hibiscus for an importer whose rule is simple: no bag may be below 1,000 g net.
steps: She picks 10 bags at random and weighs the contents: 1,012, 1,005, 998, 1,020, 1,008, 1,003, 1,015, 996, 1,010 and 1,007 g.
Total = 10,074 g, so the average = 10,074 / 10 = 1,007.4 g. The average looks fine.
But the lowest bag is 996 g and another is 998 g. Two of ten bags break the buyer's rule.
She raises her filling target to 1,010 g, re-checks every bag in the lot, tops up the light ones, and records the change.
blocks.result: The average alone would have hidden the problem. By checking the lowest weight, Hauwa fixed the lot before it left her store, at the cost of about 10 g extra per bag.

blocks.text: Pick sample bags from different points of the lot: the start, middle and end of packing, and from different drying trays or sacks. A sample taken only from the top of one sack can hide problems elsewhere. Write the date, lot number, who weighed and each weight in a lot record book, and keep it with the order file.
The export order process

An export order follows a predictable path. Writing it as a **standard operating procedure (SOP)** means you, or a helper, can follow it without forgetting a step. Each stage produces a document or a decision you keep in the order file.

blocks.title: One export order, start to finish
items: Enquiry and spec agreed
Sample sent and approved
Proforma invoice and payment terms
Production, checks, lot records
Documents and booking
Shipment, then payment confirmed
blocks.caption: Nothing moves to the next stage until the document or approval from the previous stage is in the order file.

items: Enquiry: record who asked, what product, quantity, destination and their required documents.
Sample: send a labelled sample from a real lot, keep an identical retained sample, and get written approval.
Proforma invoice: state product, quantity, unit price, Incoterm and named place, payment terms and delivery date. Production starts only after the buyer accepts it and agreed payment has arrived.
Production: make, check, weigh and record each lot against the spec.
Documents: commercial invoice, packing list, certificates; book transport with your forwarder.
Shipment and payment: send document copies to the buyer, follow the goods, and confirm payment through your bank.

blocks.text: Print the SOP and stick it on the wall of your store. When a new helper joins, train them through one real order with the SOP in hand.

takeaways: A one-page spec sheet tells the buyer exactly what they will receive and protects you in disputes
Take quality limits from the buyer's specification, never from guesses
Lot numbers and retained samples let you trace any complaint
Check the lowest bag weight, not only the average

activity.title: Draft your spec sheet and SOP
steps: Copy the seven spec sheet sections and fill them in for your chosen product
Mark any number you still need from the buyer or a laboratory
Create a lot number format and label one batch with it
Weigh 10 units from that batch and record the average and lowest weight
Write your six-stage order SOP on one page
activity.evidence: Your draft spec sheet, the weight record for 10 units and the SOP page

lessons.title: Export labels and transit-proof cartons: destination rules, allergens and shipping marks
objectives: List the information a UK or EU prepacked food label must carry
Emphasise allergens correctly and avoid misleading claims
Pack and mark cartons so they survive handling and are easy to identify
Audit an existing label and write a corrected version

blocks.text: Your Nigerian label was designed for NAFDAC and local shoppers. An export label must follow the **destination country's** law. Rules differ by country and product type, so this lesson uses the UK and EU food rules as a worked model, because they are clear, published and often asked for by diaspora shops. For other destinations, ask the buyer for their rules and check official sources.

blocks.name: label
blocks.caption: The label must speak the destination's legal language, not only yours.

blocks.text: What a UK or EU prepacked food label must show

items: The **name of the food**, describing what it really is.
The **list of ingredients**, in descending order of weight.

**Allergens** from the list of 14 legally declared allergens (these include peanuts, nuts, sesame, cereals containing gluten, milk, eggs, soya, fish and crustaceans), emphasised inside the ingredients list, for example in **bold**.
The **net quantity** in metric units (g or kg) for packs above 5 g.
A **best before** or **use by** date, plus any storage conditions or instructions for use.
The **name and address of the business** responsible; your importer will usually tell you whose details must appear.
**Country of origin** where it is required, and a **nutrition declaration** for most prepacked foods.
All information in a **language** consumers in that country understand, with mandatory text at a minimum x-height of 1.2 mm (0.9 mm on packs whose largest surface is under 80 square cm).

blocks.title: Cosmetics are different
blocks.text: Shea creams, soaps and oils sold as cosmetics in the UK or EU fall under cosmetics law, not food law. They need a responsible person based in that market, a safety assessment and notification before sale. Do not ship cosmetics for retail sale there until a buyer or partner in that market has agreed to act as responsible person.

blocks.title: Worked example: auditing a ginger and sesame mix label for a UK shop
blocks.context: For example, Ada in Enugu sells a 200 g 'Ginger Pepper Mix' (ginger, sesame, chilli, salt). A London shop wants to stock it. Her current label says: 'Ginger Pepper Mix. 100% natural, no chemicals. Net Wt 200g. Best before: 6 months from production. Made in Nigeria. NAFDAC No.'
steps: Ingredients: missing. She adds 'Ingredients: ginger, **sesame** seeds, chilli, salt' in descending weight order with sesame in bold, because sesame is one of the 14 allergens.
Date: 'six months from production' cannot be checked by a shopper. She prints an actual best before date with each lot, plus 'Store in a cool, dry place'.
Claims: 'no chemicals' is meaningless (salt is a chemical) and could mislead. She removes it.
Business details: the shop confirms the UK importer's name and address must appear; she adds it beside 'Produced in Nigeria by' her own details.
Nutrition: she asks the importer whether a nutrition declaration is needed for this product and arranges laboratory analysis if so.
She prints a test label and measures the smallest lower-case letter with a ruler to confirm it is at least 1.2 mm high.
blocks.result: Ada's corrected label carries ingredients with the allergen emphasised, a real date, storage advice, the importer's details and no misleading claims. She keeps the old and new versions in her export file with the importer's written approval.

blocks.title: Local label versus export label
items: Typical local label
Export-ready label
right: Real best before date and storage
blocks.caption: An export label adds what the destination's law requires and removes claims it does not allow.

blocks.text: Non-food products have their own label rules. Textiles sold in the UK and EU, such as scarves and garments, must show their **fibre composition** (for example 100% cotton). Ask your buyer which care, origin and safety marks they need for crafts, bags or jewellery.
Cartons that survive the journey

Your goods will be lifted, stacked, dropped and possibly left in humid sheds. Use **new double-wall corrugated cartons** of the right size, so items cannot move inside. Line cartons with a plastic liner for dried foods that can absorb moisture. Fill empty space. Seal with strong packing tape in an H pattern on top and bottom. Do not exceed a weight one person can lift safely; many forwarders prefer cartons under about 20 to 25 kg.

Before your first shipment, run a simple **home drop test**: pack one carton exactly as you will ship it and drop it from about waist height onto a hard floor on its bottom, one corner, one edge and one side. Open it. Any burst bag, cracked jar or crushed corner means you need better inner protection. This is not a certified test, but it catches most weak packing.
Shipping marks

Mark every carton clearly on two sides with: buyer (consignee) name and city, destination, your reference or order number, carton number such as **1/6, 2/6**, gross and net weight, lot number, 'Made in Nigeria', and handling symbols such as 'This way up' and 'Keep dry' where they apply. The same carton numbers and weights must match your packing list exactly.

takeaways: Export labels follow the destination's law; use official guidance and the buyer's rules
UK and EU food labels need ingredients, emphasised allergens, net quantity, a real date and business details
Cosmetics for UK or EU retail need a responsible person in that market
Pack in sized double-wall cartons, drop-test them and mark every carton to match the packing list

activity.title: Audit your label and test a carton
steps: Photograph your current label and list what is missing against the destination rules
Remove any claim you cannot prove, such as 'cures' or 'no chemicals'
Draft the corrected label text and check the allergen emphasis
Pack one carton as for export, drop-test it on four faces and record what happened
Write the shipping marks for that carton
activity.evidence: Before and after label drafts, your drop-test notes and a photo of the marked carton

lessons.title: Building an export price: cost per kg, Incoterms, currency buffer and freight
objectives: Build up an export cost from ex-works cost to a named handover point
Explain who carries cost and risk under EXW, FCA, FOB, CIF and DAP
Convert a naira price into a foreign-currency quote with a buffer
Write a quote that names the Incoterm, place and version

blocks.text: Many first exports lose money because the price was set from the local price plus 'something'. An export price is **built up** from your real costs, then the costs of getting goods to the point where the buyer takes over, then your margin. The point where the buyer takes over is defined by an **Incoterm**.
Incoterms in plain words

**Incoterms** are rules published by the International Chamber of Commerce (ICC). The current version is **Incoterms 2020**, with 11 rules. Each rule says which tasks, costs and risks belong to the seller and which to the buyer, and where risk passes. They do not set the price or say when the buyer must pay; you agree those separately. Seven rules suit any transport mode (EXW, FCA, CPT, CIP, DAP, DPU, DDP) and four are only for sea and inland waterway (FAS, FOB, CFR, CIF).

head: Rule
Seller delivers when
Good for a small exporter?
rows: EXW Ex Works (named place)
Goods are ready at your premises; the buyer does everything else, even export clearance
Easy for you, but the buyer may struggle with Nigerian export formalities; use with care
FCA Free Carrier (named place)
Goods are handed to the buyer's carrier at the named place, export-cleared
Often the best first choice: your costs stop at a place you know, such as your forwarder's warehouse
FOB Free On Board (named port)
Goods are on board the vessel at the named port
Sea only; for containers ICC guidance points to FCA instead
CIF Cost, Insurance and Freight (named port)
Goods are on board at the loading port, but you pay freight and minimum insurance to the destination port
Sea only; you pay to the destination but risk passes at loading
DAP Delivered at Place (named place)
Goods arrive at the buyer's named place, ready for unloading, not import-cleared
You carry the risk all the way; use only when you know the costs well

blocks.name: calculator
blocks.alt: A large calculator with a person working out numbers
blocks.caption: Every cost up to the Incoterm handover point must be inside your price.

blocks.title: Worked example: quoting 500 kg of dried ginger
blocks.context: For example, Amina in Kaduna is quoting 500 kg of dried split ginger to a UK importer. All figures are examples for practice; she uses her own records and real quotes.
steps: Ex-works cost: fresh ginger, peeling, drying and labour N2,400 per kg plus packing N150 per kg = N2,550 per kg (N1,275,000 for 500 kg).

Costs to the FCA point (her forwarder's warehouse in Lagos): road transport from Kaduna N180,000 plus documents (phytosanitary certificate, certificate of origin, forwarder's document fee) N120,000 = N300,000, or N300,000 / 500 = N600 per kg.
FCA cost = 2,550 + 600 = N3,150 per kg. She adds a 20% margin: 3,150 x 1.20 = N3,780 per kg (N1,890,000 in total).

The importer wants pounds. Suppose her bank's rate on the day is N2,000 to £1: 3,780 / 2,000 = £1.89 per kg. She adds a 5% currency buffer in case the naira strengthens before payment: 1.89 x 1.05 = £1.98 per kg (rounded). FCA Lagos price: £1.98 per kg.

The importer also asks for CIF Felixstowe. Her forwarder quotes, for example, £350 sea freight for the lot and £15 insurance: 350 / 500 = £0.70 and 15 / 500 = £0.03 per kg. CIF = 1.98 + 0.70 + 0.03 = £2.71 per kg, or £1,355 for 500 kg.
blocks.result: Amina quotes two clear options: '£1.98 per kg FCA Lagos (forwarder's warehouse address), Incoterms 2020' and '£2.71 per kg CIF Felixstowe, Incoterms 2020', each valid for 14 days. Both cover all her costs and margin.

blocks.title: How an export price is built
items: Margin and currency buffer
Freight and insurance (CIF only)
Transport and documents to handover
Packing for export
Product cost per kg
blocks.caption: Each layer sits on the one below; leaving one out turns a 'good' order into a loss.

blocks.title: Under CIF the risk still passes at Lagos
blocks.text: Under CIF you pay freight to the destination port, but the risk of loss passes to the buyer once the goods are on board at the loading port. Buyers sometimes misunderstand this. Write the Incoterm, the named place and 'Incoterms 2020' on every quote and proforma invoice so there is no argument later.
Freight charged by size, not only weight

Air carriers and couriers charge on the **chargeable weight**: the higher of the actual weight and the volumetric weight. Volumetric weight in kg is length x width x height in cm divided by a factor; 6,000 is common for air cargo and 5,000 for many express couriers. Ask your forwarder which factor they use. Light, bulky goods such as folded textiles and dried leaves are often charged on volume, so pack them tightly.
Quote validity and price checks

Give each quote a short **validity period**, for example 14 or 30 days, because freight rates and exchange rates move. Before accepting an order, re-check freight and the exchange rate. Finally, compare your price with what the product sells for in the destination: if the shop price there is lower than your landed cost, the market or the product needs rethinking.

takeaways: Build export prices up from cost: product, packing, transport and documents, freight if included, then margin
Incoterms 2020 has 11 rules; FCA at a named place is a sensible first choice for many small exporters
Always name the Incoterm, the place and 'Incoterms 2020' on quotes
Add a currency buffer and a validity period, and check chargeable weight for bulky goods

activity.title: Build your first export quote
steps: Write your ex-works cost per unit or per kg from your records
List the costs to your chosen handover point and divide by the shipment quantity
Add your margin and convert to the buyer's currency at today's bank rate plus a buffer
Write the quote line with Incoterm, named place, 'Incoterms 2020' and validity
activity.evidence: A costing sheet showing every line and the final quote sentence

quiz.q: Hauwa weighs 10 bags declared at 1,000 g. The average is 1,007 g but one bag is 994 g. Her buyer allows no bag under 1,000 g. What should she do?
options: Ship, because the average is above 1,000 g
Raise the fill target, re-check and top up every bag in the lot
Change the label to 990 g on all bags without telling the buyer
Remove the light bag from the sample and recalculate
quiz.explain: The buyer's rule is about every bag. She must fix the lot and adjust her process so light bags do not recur.

quiz.q: Which change does a UK label for a sesame-containing spice mix need?
options: Sesame emphasised, for example in bold, within the ingredients list
The words 'no chemicals' to reassure shoppers
quiz.explain: Sesame is one of the 14 allergens that must be emphasised in the ingredients list. Net quantity is given in metric units.

quiz.q: Under CIF Felixstowe, when does the risk of loss pass to the buyer?
options: When the goods arrive in Felixstowe
When the goods are on board the vessel at the loading port
When the goods leave the seller's store
quiz.explain: Under CIF the seller pays freight and minimum insurance to the destination port, but risk passes once the goods are on board at the port of shipment.

quiz.q: Amina's FCA cost is N3,150 per kg and she wants a 20% margin. The rate is N2,000 to £1 and she adds a 5% buffer. What is her price per kg?
A carton is 60 x 40 x 40 cm and weighs 6 kg. The forwarder uses a factor of 6,000. What is the chargeable weight?
quiz.explain: 60 x 40 x 40 = 96,000. 96,000 / 6,000 = 16 kg, which is higher than the actual 6 kg, so 16 kg is charged.

quiz.q: Funke sells shea body butter and a London shop wants to stock it. What must be in place first?
options: A responsible person in the UK, a safety assessment and notification before sale
Nothing, because cosmetics are not regulated
quiz.explain: Cosmetics for UK retail fall under cosmetics law, which requires a UK responsible person, a safety assessment and notification.

modules.title: Buyers, the First Shipment and Your 90-Day Plan
modules.overview: This module takes you from a prepared product to money in your account. You learn how to find and check buyers and choose safe payment terms, how to run a first shipment with your forwarder and a trained team, and how to turn everything into a 90-day plan that closes your remaining gaps.

lessons.title: Finding real buyers, sending samples and choosing safe payment terms
objectives: Name practical channels for meeting genuine foreign buyers
Verify a buyer before sending samples or goods
Rank common payment methods by risk to the exporter
Respond to a buyer enquiry with a clear, safe next step

blocks.text: A buyer is not real until you have checked who they are and agreed how you will be paid. New exporters lose more money to poor payment terms and fake buyers than to shipping accidents. This lesson gives you a calm, repeatable way to find buyers and protect yourself.

blocks.name: handshake
blocks.caption: A good export deal starts with a verified buyer and payment terms both sides understand.

blocks.text: Where small exporters meet buyers

items: **NEPC** services for registered exporters, including market information, training and matching exporters with potential buyers.
**Diaspora shops, caterers and churches** abroad that already sell Nigerian foods and fabrics. Relatives and friends abroad can visit shops with your sample and spec sheet.
**Trade fairs and exhibitions**, at home and abroad, where importers look for new suppliers. Go with samples, spec sheets and a printed price list showing Incoterms.
**Cooperatives and larger exporters** who already ship and need more supply of a product you make well. Selling through them can be your first, lower-risk export.

blocks.text: Checking a buyer

items: Get the full company name, registration number, address, website and the person's role.
Check the company register in their country; for UK companies, Companies House search is free online.
Compare email domains: a real importer rarely uses only a free email address for big orders.
Hold a video call and ask practical questions: which products they already import, from where, which port, which documents their customs ask for.
Ask for a trade reference, such as another supplier they buy from.

blocks.text: Payment methods, from safest to riskiest for you

head: Method
How it works
Risk to you
rows: Cash in advance
Buyer pays all (or an agreed deposit) before you ship
Lowest; the buyer carries the risk, so new buyers may only agree to a deposit
Letter of credit
Buyer's bank promises to pay if you present documents that match the credit exactly
Low if your documents match; banks charge fees and small spelling errors can delay payment
Documentary collection
Banks exchange your shipping documents for payment or a signed promise to pay
Medium; the buyer can refuse the documents and leave goods at the port
Open account
You ship and send an invoice; the buyer pays later, for example in 30 or 60 days
Highest; use only with buyers you know and trust

blocks.title: Payment risk for the exporter
items: Open account: highest risk
Documentary collection
Letter of credit
Cash in advance: lowest risk
blocks.caption: With a new buyer, stay near the bottom of the pyramid; move up only after several paid orders.

blocks.text: For small first orders, a common compromise is a **deposit** (for example 50%) before production and the **balance** before goods are released or before shipping. Receive foreign payments into your business account through your bank, and keep the Form NXP and bank advice in the order file.
Answering an enquiry well

Reply to serious enquiries within one or two working days, in clear and polite English, from a business email address. Attach your spec sheet, a price list naming the Incoterm and place, your minimum order, your realistic monthly capacity and your standard payment terms. Ask the buyer's required documents in the same message. A complete, organised first reply sets you apart from many suppliers who answer with only a price.
Samples

Send samples from a real lot, labelled exactly as the final product, with your spec sheet and price list. Many exporters ask unknown buyers to pay the courier cost for samples; serious buyers usually agree. Check the destination's rules even for samples: food and plant samples may still need correct labelling or documents.

blocks.title: Worked example: an enquiry that needs care
blocks.context: For example, Chioma in Aba receives a WhatsApp message: a man says he represents a 'major Canadian importer', wants 5 tonnes of dried hibiscus monthly, and asks her to send 10 kg of free samples and pay a 'supplier registration fee' to his agent.
steps: She notes the warning signs: very large volume with no questions about quality, a free-sample demand for 10 kg, and a fee to be paid to a third party.
She replies politely asking for the company's full name, registration number, website and the buyer's role, and proposes a video call.
She offers a 200 g sample from lot HB-2611-03, courier cost paid by the buyer, plus her spec sheet and a price list on FCA Lagos terms.
She states that she does not pay supplier registration fees and that first orders require a 50% deposit, with the balance before shipment.
blocks.result: The 'buyer' stops replying. Chioma lost nothing. A genuine importer who contacts her later accepts the paid sample, the video call and the deposit terms.

blocks.title: Protect your accounts
blocks.text: Never share your bank PIN, internet banking passwords or one-time codes with a buyer, agent or 'bank officer'. Confirm changes of payment instructions by phone on a number you already know, because fraudsters copy email threads and send fake 'new bank details'.

takeaways: Use NEPC, diaspora networks, trade fairs and established exporters to meet buyers
Check the company register, email domain and a video call before trusting a buyer
Cash in advance is safest for you; open account is riskiest
Paid, labelled samples from a real lot filter out most time-wasters

activity.title: Prepare your buyer and payment rules
steps: List three buyer channels you can actually reach this month
Write your five buyer-check questions as a reusable message
Decide your standard first-order payment terms and write them in one sentence
Prepare a sample pack: labelled product, spec sheet, price list with Incoterms
activity.evidence: Your buyer-check message, payment terms sentence and a photo of your sample pack

lessons.title: Running the first shipment: forwarder, documents, chargeable weight and team roles
objectives: Explain what a freight forwarder does and what to ask before booking
Prepare a matching commercial invoice and packing list
Calculate chargeable weight for an air shipment
Assign shipment roles and a two-person document check to your team

blocks.text: Your first shipment is a test of everything you prepared. Most problems at this stage come from small mismatches: a weight on the invoice that differs from the packing list, a missing certificate, or a buyer name spelt differently on two documents. A good forwarder and a disciplined team prevent most of them.

blocks.name: container-ship
blocks.caption: Whether by sea or air, your goods travel with a set of documents that must all agree.

blocks.text: Working with a freight forwarder

A **freight forwarder** arranges transport for you: booking space with airlines or shipping lines, preparing or checking transport documents, and often arranging export customs clearance through a licensed customs agent. Ask before booking: Which documents do you need from me and by when? What exactly is in your quote, and what is extra? What volumetric factor do you use? Where and when must cartons be delivered? Who clears export customs?
The core document set

items: **Commercial invoice**: seller, buyer, description, HS code, quantity, unit price, total, currency, Incoterm and named place, country of origin.
**Packing list**: each carton number, contents, net and gross weight, dimensions. It must match the carton marks.
**Transport document**: an air waybill for air freight or a bill of lading for sea freight, issued by the carrier or forwarder.
**Certificates** your buyer's country requires, for example a phytosanitary certificate and a certificate of origin.
**Form NXP** and related bank documents for the export proceeds.

blocks.title: Worked example: chargeable weight for a mixed air shipment
blocks.context: For example, Ngozi in Lagos ships to a buyer by air through a forwarder using a factor of 6,000. She has 6 cartons of dried ginger (each 50 x 40 x 30 cm, 14 kg) and 1 carton of adire scarves (60 x 40 x 40 cm, 6 kg).
steps: Ginger carton volume: 50 x 40 x 30 = 60,000 cubic cm. Volumetric weight = 60,000 / 6,000 = 10 kg. Actual weight 14 kg is higher, so each is charged at 14 kg; 6 cartons = 84 kg.
Scarf carton volume: 60 x 40 x 40 = 96,000 cubic cm. Volumetric weight = 96,000 / 6,000 = 16 kg. Actual weight is only 6 kg, so it is charged at 16 kg.
Total actual weight = 84 + 6 = 90 kg. Total chargeable weight = 84 + 16 = 100 kg.
She asks whether the scarves can go in a smaller box. Folded tightly into a 40 x 30 x 30 cm carton (36,000 cubic cm), the volumetric weight is 36,000 / 6,000 = 6 kg, equal to the actual weight.
blocks.result: Repacking the scarves cuts the chargeable weight from 100 kg to 90 kg, saving 10 kg of freight on one shipment with no change to the goods.

blocks.title: One spelling, everywhere
blocks.text: Copy the buyer's name, address and the product description from one master sheet into every document. Banks paying under a letter of credit and customs officers compare documents line by line, and a small difference can delay payment or clearance.
Team roles for an export order

Even a team of three can work like an export company if each person knows their role. Export orders are less forgiving than local ones, so explain to helpers why: a shortcut that a local customer would forgive can mean goods refused at a foreign port.

head: Role
Responsibilities
Sign-off
rows: Production lead
Makes each lot to the spec, keeps lot records and retained samples
Signs the lot record
Packing lead
Weighs, packs, drop-tests, marks cartons and fills the packing list
Signs the packing list
Documents lead (often the owner)
Prepares invoice, gets certificates, works with forwarder and bank
Signs the final document check
Second checker
Independently compares every document with the cartons and the master sheet
Initials the checklist

blocks.title: Pre-shipment document check
items: Names and addresses match everywhere
Weights match packing list and cartons
Incoterm and place on invoice
Certificates attached and in date
Copies sent to buyer
blocks.caption: Two people tick each line separately before cartons leave your store.

blocks.text: After the goods leave

Ask your forwarder for the air waybill or bill of lading number as soon as it is issued, and send scans of the invoice, packing list, certificates and transport document to the buyer on the same day. Follow the shipment with the tracking number until it arrives. If you agreed CIF or CIP, keep the insurance certificate in the file. If you sold FCA, remind the buyer that insurance from the handover point is their choice and cost. Treat the buyer's contact details and order information as confidential business data.

Train helpers by walking them through a real order using the SOP from Module 2, then let them do the next one while you check. Keep a **shipment file** for every order: quote, proforma, lot records, packing list, invoice, certificates, transport document, bank records and any photos of the cartons. This file is your proof of capability for future buyers and for NEPC.

takeaways: A forwarder books transport and handles or checks documents; ask what the quote includes
Commercial invoice, packing list, carton marks and certificates must all agree
Chargeable weight is the higher of actual and volumetric weight; tight packing saves money
Give each team member a role and make a second person check every document

activity.title: Prepare a practice shipment file
steps: Ask one forwarder for a written quote and list what it includes
Draft a commercial invoice and packing list for a practice order of your product
Calculate chargeable weight for your planned cartons
Assign the four roles to real people, even if you hold two of them
Have someone else check your two documents against the checklist
activity.evidence: The forwarder's quote, your draft invoice and packing list, and the signed checklist

lessons.title: Your 90-day export readiness plan, group supply and growth after the first order
objectives: Turn your gap list into a dated 90-day plan with costs
Decide whether to export alone or with other producers
Use your first shipment to win the next buyer
Assemble an export readiness portfolio

blocks.text: You now have the pieces: a chosen product and market, a gap check, a spec sheet and SOP, an export label draft, a price build-up, buyer and payment rules and a shipment checklist. The last step is to put them in order with dates, owners and money, so that in 90 days you are ready for a first shipment instead of 'still preparing'.

blocks.name: timeline
blocks.alt: A person arranging events along a timeline
blocks.caption: A 90-day plan turns a list of gaps into dated steps you can actually finish.

blocks.text: Alone or together?

Some products only become exportable at volume: for example dried hibiscus or ginger by sea. If your worst-month output is far below what importers order, consider **group supply**: several producers making the same product to one shared specification, with shared lot records, checked by one quality lead and sold under one exporter's name or a registered cooperative. The agreement must be written down: who checks quality, how weights are recorded, how payment is shared, and what happens to a lot that fails the spec.

If you form a group, decide its legal form early. A registered cooperative society (registered with your state's cooperative department) or a company registered with CAC can hold the bank account, sign export contracts and be the registered exporter with NEPC. An informal group with no legal identity cannot easily do these things, and members have little protection if a payment goes wrong.
Light, high-value products such as adire, beadwork or small batches of a speciality spice can often start alone, with small air or courier shipments to diaspora shops, and grow from there.
Building the plan

Take every gap from your Module 1 checklist and every 'still to confirm' note from Module 2. Put each on a line with an action, an owner, a target week and an estimated cost from a real quote. Group them into three 30-day blocks: **Days 1 to 30** for registrations and questions to the buyer and regulators, **Days 31 to 60** for product work (spec, tests, labels, packaging), and **Days 61 to 90** for a paid sample, a final quote and a practice shipment file.

blocks.title: Your 90 days
items: Days 1-30: registrations and questions
Days 31-60: spec, tests, labels
Days 61-90: sample, quote, shipment file
Day 90: ready to ship
blocks.caption: Each block depends on the one before it, so start registrations first because they take the longest to confirm.

blocks.title: Worked example: Amina's 90-day plan for ginger to Ghana
blocks.context: For example, Amina (dried ginger, Kaduna, first market Ghana) turns her gaps into a plan. Costs are her own example estimates from quotes, not fixed prices.
steps: Week 1: register on the NEPC e-registration portal (owner: Amina; fee as shown on the portal).
Week 2: email the Accra buyer asking which documents Ghana requires; ask NAQS about phytosanitary inspection (owner: Amina; cost N0).
Weeks 5 to 7: finalise spec sheet with the buyer's limits and send one lot for laboratory testing if the buyer requires it (owner: Amina; estimate N150,000).
Week 8: print revised labels and 50 cartons, drop-test one (owner: her sister Hadiza as packing lead; estimate N85,000).
Weeks 9 to 10: send a paid 1 kg sample and FCA quote (owner: Amina; courier paid by buyer).

Weeks 11 to 12: build the practice shipment file with forwarder quote and checklist (owner: Amina and Hadiza; estimate N20,000). Total estimated budget: 150,000 + 85,000 + 20,000 = N255,000 plus NEPC fees.
blocks.result: Amina has a dated plan with owners and a budget of about N255,000 plus registration fees. Each Friday she ticks off what is done and moves anything late to a new date with a reason.

blocks.title: Measure progress honestly
blocks.text: Track three numbers each month: gaps closed versus gaps remaining, money spent versus budget, and buyer conversations started. If a gap stays open for more than a month, find out why and ask for help early, for example from NEPC or a producer who already exports.

Review the plan with someone else once a month, for example a trusted fellow producer or a WODDI mentor. Saying your progress aloud to another person makes slipping dates visible early, and they may know a shortcut or contact you do not.
After the first shipment

Ask the buyer for written feedback on quality, packaging and documents. Fix what they mention before the next order. Keep the shipment file complete; with the buyer's permission, a short reference from a satisfied first buyer is powerful evidence for the next one. Only then add a second market or product, repeating the method you have learned.
Your export readiness portfolio

items: Product choice table and market scorecard with sources and dates
Gap check and copies of registrations held
Spec sheet, SOP, lot record and weight check
Export label draft and carton marking
Price build-up and quote with Incoterm
Buyer-check message, payment terms and the 90-day plan

takeaways: Turn every gap into an action with an owner, a week and a cost
Group supply under a written agreement can make bulk products exportable
Plan in three 30-day blocks: registrations, product work, then sample and shipment file
After each shipment, collect buyer feedback and fix issues before growing

activity.title: Write your 90-day plan
steps: Gather your gap check and every 'to confirm' note from earlier lessons
Write each as an action with owner, target week and estimated cost
Group actions into the three 30-day blocks and add up the budget
Decide whether you will export alone or with others, and why
Put your portfolio documents into one folder with a contents page
activity.evidence: Your 90-day plan with budget total and the portfolio contents page

quiz.q: A new buyer you have never traded with wants 60 days to pay after delivery. Which payment method is this, and how risky is it for you?
quiz.explain: Shipping first and being paid later is open account, the riskiest method. Use it only with buyers you know.

quiz.q: A carton is 50 x 40 x 30 cm and weighs 14 kg. With a factor of 6,000, what is its chargeable weight?
quiz.explain: Volumetric weight is 60,000 / 6,000 = 10 kg. The actual 14 kg is higher, so 14 kg is charged.

quiz.q: Ngozi's invoice says 90 kg gross, but her packing list says 92 kg. What should she do before shipping?
options: Ship; small differences do not matter
Re-weigh the cartons, correct the wrong document and have a second person re-check
Delete the weight from both documents
Change the carton marks to 91 kg
quiz.explain: Documents must agree with each other and with the cartons. Re-weigh, correct and get an independent second check.

quiz.q: Bisi's dried hibiscus output is 150 kg a month, but importers order by the container. What is a sensible route?
options: Promise container loads and buy from anyone to fill them
Form a group supply with producers using one written specification and quality check
quiz.explain: Group supply under a shared spec and written agreement is how small producers reach export volumes without lowering quality.

quiz.q: In a 90-day plan, why do registrations usually go in the first 30 days?
options: They often take the longest to confirm and other steps depend on them
Labels must be printed before registering
quiz.explain: Registrations and questions to regulators can take time and unlock later steps, so start them first.

quiz.q: Before Chioma pays a freight invoice, an email that looks like it is from her forwarder says their bank details have changed. What should she do?
options: Pay into the new account at once
Reply to the same email to confirm
Phone the forwarder on a number she already had to confirm before paying
Stop using that forwarder without asking
quiz.explain: Fraudsters copy email threads. Confirm payment changes on a number you already know, never through the email that announced the change.

finalQuiz.q: Which product is usually the easiest first air-freight export for a small producer?
options: A cheap, heavy bag of raw nuts
A liquid soap in a glass bottle
finalQuiz.explain: Light, stable, high-value products that are not food or cosmetics carry freight costs easily and face fewer product rules.

finalQuiz.q: A packed jar weighs 0.5 kg and sells for N5,000. Air freight is N8,000 per kg. What share of price is freight?
Which free tool shows which countries import a product and from where?
finalQuiz.explain: Trade Map by the International Trade Centre shows import and export flows by HS code.

finalQuiz.q: Who processes Form NXP for a Nigerian exporter?
options: The exporter's bank in Nigeria, under CBN rules
finalQuiz.explain: Form NXP is processed through the exporter's bank under Central Bank of Nigeria rules, recording the export and its expected proceeds.

finalQuiz.q: Why keep a retained sample of each lot?
options: To sell later at a discount
To compare against the product if a complaint arrives
To use as a free sample for new buyers
finalQuiz.explain: A retained sample lets you check whether a fault started in production or later in transit or storage.

finalQuiz.q: Which of these is NOT acceptable on a UK food label?
options: Sesame in bold in the ingredients
finalQuiz.explain: 'No chemicals' is meaningless and can mislead. The other three are required or correct practice.

finalQuiz.q: Under FCA Lagos (forwarder's warehouse), where do the seller's costs and risk usually stop?
options: When goods are handed to the buyer's carrier at that warehouse, export-cleared
When goods are loaded on the ship
At the producer's own door, without export clearance
finalQuiz.explain: FCA means delivery to the carrier at the named place, cleared for export.
There are 11 rules: 7 for any mode of transport and 4 for sea and inland waterway only.

finalQuiz.q: Kemi's FCA cost is N4,000 per unit; she adds 25% margin, the rate is N2,000 to US$1 and she adds a 5% buffer. What is her price?
Which payment method is safest for an exporter with a new buyer?
options: Cash in advance or a deposit with balance before shipment
finalQuiz.explain: Being paid before goods leave your control carries the least risk for the exporter.

finalQuiz.q: Six ginger cartons weigh 14 kg each and have a volumetric weight of 10 kg each. One scarf carton weighs 6 kg with a volumetric weight of 16 kg. What is the total chargeable weight?
finalQuiz.explain: Each carton is charged on its higher figure: 6 x 14 = 84 kg plus 16 kg = 100 kg.

finalQuiz.q: Amina's 90-day plan has a lab test (N150,000), labels and cartons (N85,000) and a shipment file (N20,000). What is her budget before registration fees?

capstone.title: Export Readiness Plan
capstone.brief: Produce an export readiness portfolio for one product and one target market: an export-standard specification and label draft, researched market requirements and a priced quote, and a costed 90-day plan naming the gaps to close before a first shipment.
steps: Choose one product using the freight-share table and the five export tests
Score three markets, choose one and record its requirements with sources and dates
Complete the Nigerian export base gap check and start any missing registration
Write the spec sheet, lot system and SOP, and weigh-check one lot
Draft the destination-compliant label and mark and drop-test one carton
Build a price from cost to an FCA (and if asked, CIF) quote naming Incoterms 2020
Write your buyer-check message and payment terms, and a 90-day plan with budget
evidence: Product choice table and market scorecard with sources
Gap check list and copies of registrations held
Spec sheet, SOP and weight record
Before and after label drafts and a photo of the marked carton
Price build-up sheet and written quote
90-day plan with owners, weeks and budget total
